title: Explain the Facade design pattern (a simplified interface to a complex subsystem) with use cases.
shortTitle: Explain the Facade design pattern with use cases

s1_definition.profdef: The Facade is a structural design pattern that provides a single, simplified, higher-level interface to a complex subsystem made of many classes. The facade does not add new functionality; it coordinates and delegates to the subsystem classes so that clients depend only on the simple facade instead of on many moving parts. This reduces coupling between the client and the subsystem, makes the common use cases easy to call, and leaves the subsystem free to change internally as long as the facade's interface stays stable.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh wants a home loan from National Bank of India. Behind the scenes a home loan involves many departments: credit-score checks, income verification, property valuation, legal title checks, and disbursement. Rajesh does not want to visit five departments and coordinate them himself. Instead he goes to one Loan Relationship Manager, tells her "I want a home loan", and she quietly coordinates all five departments and comes back with a decision. That relationship manager is the facade: one simple front person hiding a complicated process, so the customer deals with one point of contact instead of the whole machinery.
s1_definition.oneliner: A facade is one simple front door that coordinates a complicated subsystem behind it, so clients call one easy method instead of wiring together many classes themselves.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Facade is a structural design pattern that provides a single, simplified, higher-level interface to a complex subsystem made of many classes. The facade does not add new functionality; it coordinates and delegates to the subsystem classes so that clients depend only on the simple facade instead of on many moving parts. This reduces coupling between the client and the subsystem, makes the common use cases easy to call, and leaves the subsystem free to change internally as long as the facade's interface stays stable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh wants a home loan from National Bank of India. Behind the scenes a home loan involves many departments: credit-score checks, income verification, property valuation, legal title checks, and disbursement. Rajesh does not want to visit five departments and coordinate them himself. Instead he goes to one Loan Relationship Manager, tells her "I want a home loan", and she quietly coordinates all five departments and comes back with a decision. That relationship manager is the facade: one simple front person hiding a complicated process, so the customer deals with one point of contact instead of the whole machinery.

**One line to remember:** A facade is one simple front door that coordinates a complicated subsystem behind it, so clients call one easy method instead of wiring together many classes themselves.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is hiding complexity behind one entry point. A subsystem often grows into many collaborating classes, each doing part of a workflow, and the correct order of calls and the handling of their interactions is non-trivial. If every client has to know all those classes and the right sequence, the client becomes tightly coupled to the subsystem, duplicating orchestration logic and breaking whenever the subsystem changes. The facade solves this by exposing a small number of coarse-grained methods that represent the things clients actually want to do, and inside those methods it performs the correct sequence of calls to the subsystem.

Delegation is the mechanism. The facade holds references to the subsystem classes and, when a client calls a facade method, it delegates the real work to them in order. For example a payment facade's `pay(order)` method might call the fraud checker, then the balance checker, then the ledger, then the notifier, in the right sequence, returning one simple result. Crucially the facade adds no business rules of its own beyond orchestration; the real logic still lives in the subsystem classes, so you are not creating a God object with all the logic, you are creating a thin coordinator.

An important property is that the facade does not forbid direct access to the subsystem. Clients that need fine-grained control can still use the subsystem classes directly; the facade just offers the easy path for the common cases. This keeps the pattern non-intrusive, unlike wrapping the subsystem so tightly that advanced use becomes impossible.

The facade reduces coupling and improves changeability. Because clients depend only on the facade's interface, you can refactor, replace, or reorder the subsystem internals without touching client code, as long as the facade's method signatures and behaviour stay the same. This is the dependency-inversion benefit: clients depend on a stable abstraction, not on volatile concrete internals.

It is worth distinguishing the facade from near neighbours so you use the right pattern. A facade simplifies and unifies a subsystem but does not change interfaces to make incompatible things fit; that is the Adapter, which converts one interface into another a client expects. A facade is not a Mediator either; a mediator coordinates two-way interaction between peer objects that talk back to it, while a facade is a one-way simplification where the subsystem does not know the facade exists. And a facade is not a Proxy, which stands in for a single object to control access, caching, or laziness, whereas a facade fronts many objects. In practice an API Gateway in microservices is a facade at the network level, presenting one endpoint that fans out to many internal services.

Typical use cases: giving a clean service-layer method over a tangle of repositories, validators, calculators, and external clients; wrapping a complicated third-party library so the rest of the code calls a simple in-house interface and the library can be swapped later; providing one `onboardCustomer` or `processLoan` method that coordinates many steps; and offering a startup facade that initialises many subsystems in the right order. In Spring, a `@Service` class that orchestrates several repositories and clients to fulfil one business operation is effectively a facade.

Senior nuances worth mentioning: keep the facade thin, because if it starts holding real business rules it degrades into a God object violating single responsibility; you can have several facades over the same subsystem for different client needs rather than one bloated facade; the facade is an excellent place to apply cross-cutting concerns like a single transaction boundary, consistent logging, and uniform error translation for a whole workflow; and the pattern shines when onboarding new developers, because they can accomplish common tasks through the facade without learning the entire subsystem first.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — When National Bank of India added home loans, the loan approval workflow touched five subsystems: credit scoring, income verification, property valuation, legal title check, and disbursement. Every part of the app that wanted to process a loan had to call all five in the right order, and this orchestration logic was copied in several places and broke whenever a step changed. This is exactly what a facade solves, by putting that orchestration in one place behind one simple method.

Problem 2 — Different callers wanted the simple path ("just approve this loan") while a few advanced internal tools needed to run only the credit check or only the valuation. This is exactly why a facade is non-intrusive, offering the easy coarse method while still allowing direct subsystem access for the rare advanced cases.

Problem 3 — The bank later replaced its in-house credit scorer with an external bureau, and it would have been painful to update every caller. Because callers depended only on the facade, the swap happened behind the facade with no client changes. This is exactly the decoupling benefit of a facade.

Our mini-project builds a LoanApprovalFacade over the five subsystem classes. The facade exposes one method `approveHomeLoan` that coordinates credit scoring, income verification, property valuation, legal check, and disbursement in the correct order and returns a single decision, while the subsystem classes still exist and can be called directly. The demo runs a home-loan application for Rajesh.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a home-loan application for Rajesh (SAV2001), requesting forty lakh rupees, annual income twelve lakh, property value sixty lakh.

Step 1: The client calls one method, `facade.approveHomeLoan(...)`, passing the application data. The client knows nothing about the five subsystem classes; it only sees the facade. The data at this point is the application parameters.

Step 2: Inside the facade, it delegates first to CreditScoreService, which returns a score of 760. Because 760 is at least the minimum of 700, the step passes. The data flowing is the account id in, a boolean out.

Step 3: The facade delegates to IncomeVerifier, which checks that forty lakh is at most five times twelve lakh, that is sixty lakh. Forty lakh is within sixty lakh, so the step passes.

Step 4: The facade delegates to PropertyValuer, which computes the maximum loan as eighty percent of sixty lakh, that is forty-eight lakh. The requested forty lakh is within forty-eight lakh, so the loan-to-value check passes.

Step 5: The facade delegates to LegalTitleChecker, which confirms the title is clear. All four checks have now passed in the correct order, which is the orchestration the facade owns.

Step 6: The facade delegates to DisbursementService, which disburses forty lakh to SAV2001 and returns a reference. The facade assembles one simple result string, "APPROVED and DISBURSED, ref ...", and returns it to the client. The client receives a single clean answer despite five subsystems having run.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:10:40 INFO    FACADE approveHomeLoan for Rajesh Kumar amount Rs.4000000
2026-10-24 15:10:40 INFO    disbursed Rs.4000000 to SAV2001 ref LN-1766570440123
2026-10-24 15:10:40 INFO    FINAL DECISION for Rajesh: APPROVED and DISBURSED, ref LN-1766570440123
```

```

    │  (client depends ONLY on the facade)
    ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           LoanApprovalFacade                  │  ← one simple front door
  │  orchestrates in the correct order:           │
  └───┬──────┬──────────┬──────────┬───────────┬──┘
      │      │          │          │           │
      ▼      ▼          ▼          ▼           ▼
  Credit   Income    Property    Legal      Disbursement
  Score    Verifier  Valuer      Title      Service
  760≥700  40L≤60L   40L≤48L     clear      disburse 40L
   ✓        ✓         ✓           ✓          ref LN-...
      │      │          │          │           │
      └──────┴──────────┴──────────┴───────────┘
                     │ single result
                     ▼
  Response to client: "APPROVED and DISBURSED, ref LN-..."

  ── Rejection path (any check fails) ──
  Credit 640 < 700 → facade returns "REJECTED: low credit score"
  (no further subsystems called — short-circuit)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Facade is a structural pattern that gives clients one simple, higher-level interface to a complex subsystem of many classes. The facade does not add business logic of its own; it coordinates and delegates to the subsystem in the correct order, so clients depend on one easy entry point instead of on many moving parts. That reduces coupling, makes the common workflows trivial to call, and lets the subsystem evolve internally as long as the facade's interface stays stable.

The mechanism is delegation. The facade holds references to the subsystem classes, and when a client calls a coarse-grained facade method, it performs the right sequence of calls behind the scenes and returns one simple result. Importantly the facade is non-intrusive: it offers the easy path for common cases, but advanced callers can still use the subsystem classes directly, so it simplifies without imprisoning. I also keep the facade thin, because the moment it starts holding real rules it degrades into a God object and violates single responsibility.

I am careful to distinguish it from near neighbours. An Adapter converts one interface into another so incompatible things fit, a Mediator coordinates two-way interaction between peers that talk back to it, and a Proxy stands in for one object to control access or caching, whereas a facade is a one-way simplification fronting many objects that do not know it exists. At the network level, an API Gateway in microservices is essentially a facade, presenting one endpoint that fans out to many internal services.

On my project at National Bank of India the home-loan workflow touched five subsystems: credit scoring, income verification, property valuation, legal title check, and disbursement. Before the facade, every caller duplicated the orchestration and broke when a step changed. We introduced a LoanApprovalFacade with one method, approveHomeLoan, that runs the five subsystems in the correct order and returns a single decision, and it became the single transaction boundary and the one place for consistent logging and error handling. The payoff was concrete: when we later replaced our in-house credit scorer with an external bureau, we changed only the facade's wiring and not a single caller, because everyone depended on the facade's stable interface.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that a facade is one simple front door that orchestrates a complicated subsystem behind it, reducing coupling and making common tasks easy, while still letting advanced callers reach the subsystem directly, and the key discipline is to keep the facade thin so it coordinates without becoming a God object.
